# How to use this guide

Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry II builds on Pharmacognosy I. Unit 1 is theory (how plants make their chemicals), Unit 2 is a long list of drug monographs, Units 3 and 4 are about getting single compounds out of plants in the laboratory and in the factory, and Unit 5 is the toolbox of extraction and analytical techniques. Marks come from correct **biological sources with families**, correct **chemical constituents**, neat **classifications** and clean **flow diagrams** of pathways and processes.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 2 is the biggest (14 of the 45 teaching hours) and carries eight groups of drugs — spread it over three days and write each monograph out from memory. Units 3 and 4 overlap: Unit 3 is laboratory isolation and identification, Unit 4 is industrial production, estimation and use of the same kind of compounds. Study them one after the other and keep a single table for the compounds that appear in both (artemisinin, atropine, caffeine, podophyllotoxin).

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long essay (10-mark), short answer (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. Very short questions help with Section A and with quick revision.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with tables, examples and a diagram where one fits.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Metabolic pathways | Shikimic acid pathway with a flow chart; acetate–malonate and acetate–mevalonate pathways; isoprene rule and classes of terpenoids; amino acid precursors of the main alkaloid groups; tracer techniques with 14C, feeding methods and limitations |
| 2 Secondary metabolites | Monographs of vinca, rauwolfia, belladonna, opium, liquorice, dioscorea, digitalis, clove, cinnamon, mentha, fennel, coriander, catechu, senna, aloes, benzoin, asafoetida, myrrh, guggul, ginger, colophony, gentian, artemisia, taxus; definitions and classifications of alkaloids, flavonoids, tannins, resins, glycosides, volatile oils |
| 3 Isolation and identification | Isolation of caffeine, atropine, quinine, reserpine, menthol, citral, rutin; general acid–base scheme for alkaloids; identification tests (Vitali–Morin, murexide, thalleioquin, Shinoda, Keller–Killiani) |
| 4 Industrial production | Diosgenin to steroid hormones; digoxin from *Digitalis lanata*; sennosides as calcium salts; artemisinin and ACTs; paclitaxel supply problem and semi-synthesis; vincristine and vinblastine; caffeine from tea waste; estimation methods for each |
| 5 Basics of phytochemistry | Classical versus modern extraction; supercritical fluid extraction; TLC and HPTLC; paper chromatography; GC; HPLC; principles and uses of UV, IR, NMR, MS; electrophoresis |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Every monograph has the same skeleton: **synonym → biological source with family → geographical source → chemical constituents → chemical tests → uses → commercial applications → adulterants.** Write each heading even if you can manage only one line under it.
2. Write the botanical name in full the first time, genus with a capital letter and species in small letters (underline it in handwriting), followed by the family: *Catharanthus roseus*, Apocynaceae. A wrong family loses an easy mark.
3. Name the **active constituent** with its chemical class, not just the plant: "artemisinin, a sesquiterpene lactone with an endoperoxide bridge", "sennosides A and B, dianthrone glycosides".
4. For pathway questions draw the **flow chart first**, then explain it in short numbered lines. A clear chart of the shikimic acid or mevalonate pathway earns most of the marks on its own.
5. For isolation questions use a **numbered flow of steps** with the reagent and purpose at each step, and finish with identification and assay.
6. Learn the paired tests so you never mix them up: Borntrager (anthraquinones) and modified Borntrager (C-glycoside aloin); Keller–Killiani (2-deoxy sugar); Vitali–Morin (tropane esters); murexide (purine alkaloids); thalleioquin (quinine); Shinoda (flavonoids); matchstick (catechins); copper acetate (colophony); umbelliferone fluorescence (asafoetida).
7. In technique questions always give **principle → instrumentation or procedure → detection → applications**, with one real pharmacognostic example.
8. Do not confuse similar pairs: hydrolysable versus condensed tannins; cardenolides versus bufadienolides; *Digitalis purpurea* versus *D. lanata*; Sumatra versus Siam benzoin; Curacao versus Cape aloes; Tinnevelly versus Alexandrian senna; vincristine (neuropathy) versus vinblastine (bone-marrow suppression); normal versus reverse phase HPLC.
9. For practical examinations, keep the chemical tests of asafoetida, benzoin, colophony, aloes and myrrh at your fingertips: they are the usual "identify the given drug" question.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics fully: **the shikimic acid and mevalonate pathways with their products**, **the monographs of opium, belladonna, digitalis, senna and clove**, **isolation of caffeine, atropine and quinine with their identification tests**, **industrial production of diosgenin, digoxin and paclitaxel**, and **TLC, HPLC and the four spectroscopic methods**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 in one table**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Three building blocks | Acetyl-CoA (C2), shikimic acid, amino acids; isoprene C5 from mevalonate or MEP |
| Shikimic acid pathway | PEP + erythrose-4-P → DAHP → dehydroquinic → dehydroshikimic (→ gallic acid) → shikimic → EPSP → chorismic acid → phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan |
| Phenylpropanoids | PAL: phenylalanine → cinnamic acid → coumarins, lignans, eugenol, anethole, lignin |
| Flavonoids | Ring B + C3 from shikimate, ring A from 3 malonyl-CoA (chalcone synthase) |
| Acetate–malonate | Polyketides: fatty acids, anthraquinones (senna, aloes), tetracyclines |
| Acetate–mevalonate | 3 acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonic acid → IPP/DMAPP → GPP C10 → FPP C15 → GGPP C20 → squalene C30 → phytoene C40 |
| Terpene classes | Mono C10 menthol, sesqui C15 artemisinin, di C20 taxol, tri C30 glycyrrhetinic acid, tetra C40 carotenoids |
| Alkaloid precursors | Ornithine → tropanes; lysine → piperidines; tyrosine → morphine, berberine; tryptophan + secologanin → strictosidine → reserpine, vinca, quinine; histidine → pilocarpine; purines → caffeine |
| Tracers | 14C and 3H most used; feeding by roots, wick, cut shoot, injection, 14CO2, cell culture |
| Tracer methods | Precursor–product with degradation, competitive feeding, sequential (pulse) analysis, double labelling, mutants, grafting |
| Formula | % incorporation = activity in product × 100 ÷ activity fed |

| Quinine | Lime + toluene, dilute H2SO4, neutralise; quinine sulphate crystallises first |
| Reserpine | Alcohol extract, mildly alkaline pH, chloroform, alumina column |
| Caffeine | Water + lime, chloroform, sublimation |
| Podophyllotoxin | Alcohol percolate poured into acidified water → resin → chromatography |
| Curcumin | Hexane defat, acetone extract, crystallise; three yellow TLC spots |

**Unit 4 — production and use**

| Compound | Route | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forskolin | Solvent extraction of *Coleus* roots | Glaucoma, raises cAMP |
| Sennosides | Aqueous methanol, calcium salt precipitation; assay about 515 nm | Laxative |
| Artemisinin | Hexane extraction or semi-synthesis from yeast artemisinic acid | ACT for malaria |
| Diosgenin | Fermentation, acid hydrolysis, solvent extraction; Marker degradation → 16-DPA | Steroid hormones |
| Digoxin | Lanatoside C of *D. lanata*; enzymic loss of glucose, mild alkali removes acetyl | Heart failure, atrial fibrillation |
| Atropine | Acid–base extraction from *Duboisia*, *Hyoscyamus*, *Datura*, then racemisation | Mydriatic, antidote, preanaesthetic |
| Podophyllotoxin | Resin from alcohol extract, chromatography | Etoposide, teniposide, warts |
| Caffeine | Tea waste with lime, decaffeination of coffee, synthesis | Stimulant, analgesic adjuvant |
| Paclitaxel | Semi-synthesis from 10-DAB of needles; plant cell fermentation | Ovarian, breast, lung cancer |
| Vincristine, vinblastine | Alkaloid extraction and chromatography; coupling of catharanthine + vindoline | Leukaemia, lymphoma |

**Unit 5**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Extraction steps | Size reduction → wetting → dissolution → diffusion |
| Classical | Maceration, percolation, digestion, infusion, decoction, Soxhlet, counter-current, distillation, expression |
| Modern | Supercritical CO2 (31 °C, 74 bar; no residue), microwave, ultrasound, pressurised solvent, enzyme-assisted |
| Rf | Distance of solute ÷ distance of solvent front; always < 1 |
| Paper chromatography | Partition; water on cellulose; n-butanol : acetic acid : water |
| TLC | Adsorption on silica gel G; UV 254/365, iodine, anisaldehyde–H2SO4, Dragendorff; HPTLC adds densitometry |
| GC | Volatile, stable samples; carrier gas; FID; volatile oils |
| HPLC | Reverse phase C18, polar compounds elute first; PDA, fluorescence, ELSD (no chromophore), MS |
| UV | A = ε c l; conjugation; flavonoid shift reagents; caffeine 273 nm, curcumin about 425 nm |
| IR | Functional groups; fingerprint region 1500–600 cm−1 for identity |
| NMR | Chemical shift, integration, multiplicity, coupling constant; 13C and 2D for structure |
| MS | Molecular ion gives molecular weight; GC–MS and LC–MS for trace work |
| Electrophoresis | Charge and size in an electric field; agarose for DNA fingerprinting of plants, PAGE for proteins, capillary for small molecules |
| Standardisation | Identity → purity limits → fingerprint → marker assay; active versus analytical marker |

**Five facts that are easy marks**

1. Glyphosate blocks EPSP synthase of the shikimic acid pathway, which animals do not have.
2. Digoxin comes from *Digitalis lanata*, digitoxin from *D. purpurea*.
3. Atropine is racemic and optically inactive; hyoscyamine is laevorotatory.
4. Aloin is a C-glycoside, so it needs the modified Borntrager test.
5. Artemisinin has no useful UV absorption, so HPLC with an evaporative light-scattering detector is used.

# Morphology, histology, powder characteristics, extraction and detection of cinchona, cinnamon, senna, clove, ephedra, fennel and coriander

**Aim:** To study the macroscopic (morphological) features, the transverse section (histology) and the powder characteristics of cinchona, cinnamon, senna, clove, ephedra, fennel and coriander, and to extract and detect their main constituents by simple chemical tests.

> Follow your lab manual where the details differ. Draw every section and powder as a labelled diagram in your record; in the examination the diagram and labels carry most of the marks.

## Principle

An organised crude drug is identified by three things that together are hard to fake:
- **morphology** — shape, size, colour, surface, fracture, odour and taste of the whole drug;
- **histology** — the arrangement of tissues seen in a thin transverse section (TS), made clear by clearing and staining;
- **powder microscopy** — diagnostic cell types (fibres, stone cells, crystals, trichomes, stomata, oil glands, pollen) that survive powdering.

Lignified walls (fibres, stone cells, xylem) are stained **pink-red with phloroglucinol and conc. HCl**. Starch turns **blue-black with iodine**. Calcium oxalate crystals stay undissolved in acetic acid but dissolve in HCl without effervescence. Oil droplets are stained red with **Sudan III**.

The chemical tests detect the class of the active constituent (alkaloid, anthraquinone, phenolic volatile oil and so on) in a simple extract.

## Requirements

**Drugs:** cinchona bark, cinnamon bark, senna leaf, clove, ephedra stem, fennel fruit, coriander fruit (whole and powdered).

**Reagents:** chloral hydrate solution, phloroglucinol (1% in alcohol), conc. HCl, iodine solution, Sudan III, glycerine, dilute H2SO4, bromine water, dilute ammonia, ferric chloride solution, potassium hydroxide solution, benzene or chloroform, copper sulphate solution, sodium hydroxide solution, ether, 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent.

**Apparatus:** compound microscope, slides and cover slips, razor or blade, pith or potato for holding thin material, watch glasses, spirit lamp, test tubes, water bath, hand lens.

## Procedure

1. **Morphology:** examine the whole drug with the naked eye and a hand lens. Note shape, size, colour of outer and inner surfaces, fracture, odour and taste.
2. **Transverse section:** soften the drug if needed (soak barks and fruits in water; boil hard material briefly). Cut thin sections with a sharp razor, keeping the blade wet.
3. **Clearing and staining:** warm the sections in chloral hydrate to clear them. Stain with phloroglucinol, then add a drop of conc. HCl. Mount in glycerine and examine under low and then high power.
4. **Powder:** take a small quantity of powder on a slide. Mount separately in (a) chloral hydrate after warming, (b) phloroglucinol + HCl, (c) iodine, and (d) Sudan III where an oil is expected. Record the diagnostic elements.
5. **Extraction and detection:** carry out the test for each drug as given in the table at the end.

## Observations

### Cinchona (bark of *Cinchona calisaya*, *C. ledgeriana*, *C. officinalis*, *C. succirubra*; Rubiaceae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Quills or curved pieces; outer surface greyish-brown with longitudinal wrinkles and transverse cracks, often with lichens; inner surface reddish-brown and finely striated; fracture short in the outer part and fibrous in the inner part; taste intensely bitter, odourless |
| TS | Cork; cortex with idioblasts holding microcrystals (sandy crystals) of calcium oxalate; secondary phloem with **isolated, thick-walled, spindle-shaped phloem fibres** having funnel-shaped pit canals; medullary rays |
| Powder | Lignified **spindle-shaped fibres** (diagnostic), sandy crystals, cork cells, parenchyma with starch; **stone cells are absent** |

### Cinnamon (inner bark of *Cinnamomum zeylanicum*; Lauraceae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Compound quills of thin bark (about 0.5 mm thick) packed one inside the other; outer surface yellowish-brown with fine wavy lines and small scars; inner surface darker and striated; fracture splintery; odour fragrant, taste aromatic and slightly sweet |
| TS | Outer bark is scraped off, so the section starts with the **pericycle: a continuous band of stone cells with groups of pericyclic fibres**; secondary phloem with oil cells, mucilage cells, phloem fibres and medullary rays containing small **acicular crystals of calcium oxalate** |
| Powder | Stone cells (often thickened more on the inner and side walls), isolated fibres, oil cells, small simple and compound starch grains, needle crystals; no cork |

### Senna (leaflets of *Cassia angustifolia* or *C. acutifolia*; Leguminosae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Lanceolate leaflets with an acute, mucronate apex and an **asymmetric base**; entire margin; pale yellowish-green (Tinnevelly) or greyish-green (Alexandrian); faint odour, mucilaginous then slightly bitter taste |
| TS | **Isobilateral** leaf: palisade under both epidermises; epidermis with **paracytic stomata** on both surfaces and **unicellular, thick-walled, warty, curved trichomes**; midrib vascular bundle with a sheath of fibres surrounded by a **crystal sheath** of calcium oxalate prisms; cluster crystals in the spongy tissue |
| Powder | Paracytic stomata, warty unicellular trichomes, fibres with crystal sheath, prisms and clusters of calcium oxalate |

### Clove (flower buds of *Syzygium aromaticum*; Myrtaceae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Dark brown buds about 10–18 mm long; a sub-cylindrical **hypanthium** with four thick sepals and a dome-shaped head of four unopened petals enclosing stamens and a style; pressing with a fingernail squeezes out oil; strong spicy odour and pungent taste |
| TS (hypanthium) | Epidermis with thick cuticle and stomata; **large schizolysigenous oil glands in two or three rows** just beneath the epidermis; parenchyma with bicollateral vascular bundles; a loose spongy (aerenchyma) zone; central column of tissue with vascular strands; cluster crystals of calcium oxalate |
| Powder | Fragments of oil glands, **triangular (tetrahedral) pollen grains**, cluster crystals, a few fibres; **no starch and no stone cells** (stone cells point to clove stalks as an adulterant) |

### Ephedra (young stems of *Ephedra gerardiana*, *E. sinica*, *E. equisetina*; Ephedraceae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Slender, green to greyish-green, cylindrical, finely ridged and jointed stems with nodes carrying small scale-like leaves; taste slightly bitter and astringent |
| TS | Epidermis with a thick cuticle and **sunken stomata in the furrows** between the ridges; **groups of hypodermal fibres** under the ridges; chlorenchymatous cortex; pericyclic fibres; a ring of collateral vascular bundles; central pith |
| Powder | Epidermis with sunken stomata, abundant lignified fibres, fragments of green cortex, small xylem vessels |

### Fennel (cremocarps of *Foeniculum vulgare*; Umbelliferae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Oblong, greenish-yellow cremocarps about 5–10 mm long, often split into two mericarps; each mericarp with **five prominent primary ridges**; sweet anise-like odour and taste |
| TS (mericarp) | Epicarp; mesocarp with **six vittae (four on the dorsal side, two on the commissural side)** and lignified reticulate parenchyma; endocarp of narrow cells in groups lying at different angles (**parquetry layer**); testa; large endosperm with fixed oil, aleurone grains and tiny rosette crystals of calcium oxalate; carpophore in the commissure |
| Powder | Brown fragments of vittae, parquetry cells, reticulate lignified mesocarp cells, endosperm with oil globules and aleurone; Sudan III stains the oil red |

### Coriander (cremocarps of *Coriandrum sativum*; Umbelliferae)

| Feature | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Morphology | Almost spherical, straw-coloured to brown cremocarps; the two mericarps stay joined; **ten wavy primary ridges and eight straight, more prominent secondary ridges**; aromatic odour |
| TS | Epicarp; outer mesocarp in which the dorsal vittae are vestigial; inner mesocarp with a **broad band of lignified sclerenchyma (fibres)** — the diagnostic feature; only **two vittae per mericarp, on the commissural surface**; parquetry endocarp; curved endosperm (concave on the inner side) with aleurone and rosette crystals |
| Powder | Lignified fibre bundles crossing at angles, parquetry cells, endosperm cells with oil and rosette crystals, vittae fragments |

### Extraction and detection

| Drug | Extraction | Test | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cinchona | Heat 0.1 g powder in a dry test tube | **Grahe's test** | Purple-red vapours that condense as a red tar on the cooler part (quinoline alkaloids) |
| Cinchona | Shake powder with dilute H2SO4, filter | Fluorescence in UV light | Blue fluorescence (quinine, quinidine) |
| Cinchona | Same acid extract + bromine water, then excess ammonia | **Thalleioquin test** | Emerald-green colour (quinine) |
| Cinnamon | Extract with chloroform, evaporate, take the residue in alcohol | 2,4-DNPH reagent | Yellow-orange precipitate (cinnamaldehyde, an aldehyde) |
| Senna | Boil with dilute H2SO4, cool, shake with benzene or chloroform, separate the organic layer and shake it with dilute ammonia | **Borntrager's test** | Pink to red ammoniacal layer (anthraquinones) |
| Clove | Alcoholic extract or a drop of oil | Ferric chloride | Blue colour (phenol eugenol) |
| Clove | Oil + strong KOH solution | Potassium eugenate | Needle-shaped crystals |
| Ephedra | Moisten with ammonia, extract with ether, evaporate, dissolve in a little water | Copper sulphate + NaOH, then shake with ether | Violet colour; ether layer purple, water layer blue (ephedrine, Chen–Kao reaction) |
| Fennel / coriander | Section or powder mounted in Sudan III | Volatile oil in vittae | Red-stained oil droplets |

## Result

The given drugs were identified as cinchona, cinnamon, senna, clove, ephedra, fennel and coriander by their morphology, transverse section and powder characteristics, and their main constituents were detected by the tests above.

## Precautions

1. Cut sections as thin as possible and keep the razor wet.
2. Do not let chloral hydrate dry on the slide; add more as needed.
3. Add conc. HCl in small drops; wipe spilled acid off the microscope stage at once.
4. Use a fresh mount for each reagent so that colours are not confused.
5. Heat organic solvents only on a water bath, never over a flame.

## Viva questions

1. **Why are stone cells absent in genuine cinchona bark?** It has no sclereids; its strength comes from isolated spindle-shaped phloem fibres, which are diagnostic.
2. **Why is there no cork in a cinnamon section?** The outer bark (cork and cortex) is scraped off during preparation, so the drug starts at the pericycle.
3. **Name the stomata of senna.** Paracytic (rubiaceous): two subsidiary cells lying parallel to the guard cells.
4. **What does the presence of stone cells in clove powder suggest?** Adulteration with clove stalks.
5. **How do fennel and coriander differ in vittae?** Fennel has six per mericarp (four dorsal, two commissural); coriander has only two, on the commissural side.
6. **Which feature identifies coriander in a section?** A band of lignified sclerenchyma in the inner mesocarp.
7. **What is Grahe's test?** Heating cinchona bark in a dry tube gives purple-red vapours that condense as a red tar.
8. **Why does ephedrine give a poor precipitate with the usual alkaloid reagents?** It is a protoalkaloid with the nitrogen in a side chain, not in a ring; the Chen–Kao copper test is used instead.

# Isolation and detection of caffeine from tea dust

**Aim:** To isolate caffeine from tea dust, find the percentage yield and identify it by chemical tests, melting point and TLC.

> Follow your lab manual for exact quantities. Chloroform and dichloromethane are toxic: work in a fume hood, keep them away from flames and collect the used solvent for recovery.

## Principle

Tea leaves (*Camellia sinensis*, Theaceae) contain caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine), a purine alkaloid, together with tannins, flavonoids, pigments and gallic acid.

- Caffeine is fairly soluble in **hot water** and in **chloroform**, and very weakly basic.
- When tea is boiled with water containing **calcium carbonate**, the tannins and other acidic compounds form insoluble calcium salts and stay behind, while free caffeine passes into the water.
- Caffeine is then taken out of the cooled water extract into **chloroform** by liquid–liquid extraction, which leaves sugars and salts in the water.
- The crude product is purified by **sublimation** or recrystallisation, since caffeine sublimes on heating.

```text
Tea dust + water + CaCO3 ──boil, filter hot──→ aqueous extract (caffeine)
      │                                       (tannins stay as Ca salts)
      ↓
Aqueous extract ──shake with CHCl3 (3 times)──→ CHCl3 layer
      ↓ dry (Na2SO4), evaporate
Crude caffeine ──sublimation / recrystallisation──→ pure caffeine
```

## Requirements

**Chemicals:** tea dust (10 g), calcium carbonate (powdered), chloroform or dichloromethane, anhydrous sodium sulphate, acetone or ethanol, potassium chlorate, conc. HCl, dilute ammonia, tannic acid solution, Wagner's reagent, Dragendorff's reagent, caffeine standard.

**Apparatus:** 500 ml beaker or round-bottom flask, water bath, funnel and filter paper (or cloth), separating funnel, conical flasks, evaporating dish, watch glasses, melting point apparatus, TLC plates and chamber.

## Procedure

1. Weigh 10 g of tea dust into a beaker with about 4–5 g of calcium carbonate and 150 ml of water.
2. Boil gently for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then and adding water to keep the volume.
3. Filter **while hot** through cloth or a fluted filter paper. Wash the residue with a little hot water and combine the filtrates.
4. Cool the filtrate to room temperature.
5. Transfer it to a separating funnel and extract with 25 ml chloroform. **Swirl and invert gently** rather than shaking hard, to avoid an emulsion. Release pressure often.
6. Run off the lower chloroform layer. Repeat the extraction two more times with fresh chloroform.
7. Combine the chloroform extracts and dry them over anhydrous sodium sulphate.
8. Filter into a weighed dish and evaporate the solvent on a water bath (in a fume hood) to get crude caffeine, a pale greenish-white residue. Weigh it.
9. **Purification:** sublime the crude caffeine by warming it gently under an inverted funnel or a watch glass cooled from above; white needles collect on the cool surface. Or recrystallise from a little hot acetone or ethanol.
10. Dry and weigh the purified caffeine and carry out the tests.

## Identification tests

| Test | Procedure | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Murexide test** | Few crystals + a crystal of KClO3 + 1–2 drops conc. HCl; evaporate to dryness on a water bath; expose residue to ammonia vapour | Purple colour (purine alkaloid) |
| Tannic acid | Aqueous solution + tannic acid | White precipitate, soluble in excess |
| Wagner's reagent | Acidified solution + iodine in KI | Reddish-brown precipitate |
| Mayer's reagent | Acidified solution | **No precipitate** (caffeine is an exception among alkaloids) |
| Sublimation | Warm a few crystals on a slide | White needle-shaped sublimate |
| Melting point | Capillary method | Close to that of the caffeine standard (about 235–238 °C) |
| TLC | Silica gel G; spot sample and standard; develop in a system from your manual; view under UV 254 nm or spray with Dragendorff's reagent | Spot with the same Rf as standard caffeine |

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of tea dust taken (W) | 10 g |
| Weight of empty dish (W1) |  |
| Weight of dish + purified caffeine (W2) |  |
| Weight of caffeine (W2 − W1) |  |

% yield of caffeine = (W2 − W1) × 100 / W

**Worked example.** Tea dust = 10.0 g; caffeine obtained = 0.180 g.
% yield = 0.180 × 100 / 10 = **1.8% w/w**

The yield is usually less than the true caffeine content of tea, because some caffeine stays in the water layer and some is lost during sublimation.

Rf = distance travelled by the spot ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front.

## Result

Caffeine was isolated from tea dust. Yield = ___% w/w. It gave a positive murexide test, melted at ___ °C and showed a TLC spot with the same Rf as standard caffeine.

## Precautions

1. Filter the decoction while hot; caffeine is far less soluble in cold water.
2. Do not shake the separating funnel vigorously; emulsions are common with tea extracts.
3. Dry the chloroform layer completely before evaporating.
4. Evaporate chloroform only on a water bath in a fume hood.
5. Sublime with gentle heat; strong heating chars the product.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is calcium carbonate added?** To bind tannins and other acids as insoluble calcium salts, so they are not extracted, and to keep caffeine as the free base.
2. **Why is chloroform used for the second extraction?** Caffeine is much more soluble in chloroform than in cold water, while sugars and salts stay in water.
3. **Which test identifies caffeine?** The murexide test, given by purine alkaloids.
4. **Does caffeine give Mayer's test?** No; it is one of the few alkaloids that do not.
5. **Why can caffeine be purified by sublimation?** It passes from solid to vapour on heating and condenses as pure crystals.
6. **What other purine alkaloids occur in tea?** Small amounts of theophylline and theobromine.
7. **What is the industrial source of natural caffeine?** Tea waste and the caffeine removed when coffee is decaffeinated.

# Isolation and detection of diosgenin from Dioscorea

**Aim:** To isolate diosgenin from the tubers of *Dioscorea* by acid hydrolysis and solvent extraction, find the yield and identify it by chemical tests and TLC.

> Follow your lab manual for exact quantities and acid strength. Refluxing with mineral acid and handling petroleum ether need care: use a fume hood, keep solvents away from flames and wear gloves and goggles.

## Principle

*Dioscorea* tubers (family **Dioscoreaceae**; for example *D. deltoidea*, *D. floribunda*, *D. composita*) contain steroidal saponins, chiefly **dioscin**. Dioscin is a glycoside of the spirostan sapogenin **diosgenin**.

- Saponins are water-soluble because of their sugar chain; the aglycone diosgenin is insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents.
- **Acid hydrolysis** breaks the glycosidic bonds, releasing the sugars into water and leaving diosgenin in the insoluble residue.
- The washed and dried residue is extracted with **petroleum ether or hexane**, which dissolves diosgenin but not the polar plant material.
- Diosgenin crystallises when the concentrated solvent cools.

```text
Dioscin (saponin, water-soluble)
   │  dilute HCl or H2SO4, reflux
   ↓
Diosgenin (insoluble) + sugars (glucose, rhamnose, in solution)
   │  filter, wash to neutral, dry
   ↓
Residue ──petroleum ether (Soxhlet)──→ extract ──concentrate, cool──→ crude diosgenin
   ↓ recrystallise (acetone or ethanol)
Pure diosgenin
```

## Requirements

**Chemicals:** powdered dried *Dioscorea* tuber (20–25 g), dilute hydrochloric acid (about 2 N) or sulphuric acid, sodium bicarbonate or dilute ammonia, petroleum ether (60–80 °C) or hexane, acetone or ethanol, acetic anhydride, conc. H2SO4, chloroform, anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid spray, diosgenin standard (if available).

**Apparatus:** round-bottom flask with reflux condenser, heating mantle or water bath, Buchner funnel and suction, pH paper, oven, Soxhlet apparatus, evaporating dish, TLC plates and chamber, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. **Test for saponin first (optional):** shake a little powder with water in a test tube. A persistent honeycomb froth shows saponins.
2. Weigh about 20 g of powdered tuber into a round-bottom flask. Add about 150–200 ml of dilute HCl (about 2 N).
3. Reflux for 2–4 hours to hydrolyse the saponins.
4. Cool and filter under suction. Wash the residue with water until the washings are no longer acidic (check with pH paper); a little sodium bicarbonate or ammonia in the wash water helps neutralise the last traces of acid.
5. Dry the residue in an oven at about 60–80 °C.
6. Pack the dried residue in a thimble and extract with petroleum ether in a Soxhlet apparatus for about 4–6 hours.
7. Concentrate the extract on a water bath to a small volume and allow it to cool, preferably in a refrigerator. Crude diosgenin separates as a white to pale cream crystalline solid.
8. Filter, dry and weigh. Recrystallise from a small volume of acetone or ethanol if required.

## Identification tests

| Test | Procedure | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Liebermann–Burchard** | A little sample in chloroform + 1 ml acetic anhydride; add conc. H2SO4 slowly down the side | Coloured ring changing to green or blue-green (steroid nucleus) |
| **Salkowski** | Sample in chloroform + equal volume conc. H2SO4, shake and allow to separate | Red to reddish-brown colour in the chloroform layer |
| Foam test on the hydrolysed product | Shake with water | **No lasting froth** (sugars removed, so no saponin left) |
| TLC | Silica gel G; spot sample and standard; develop in a non-polar system given in your manual; spray with anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid and heat at about 105 °C | Coloured spot with the same Rf as standard diosgenin |
| Melting point | Capillary method | Compare with the diosgenin standard |

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of tuber powder (W) |  |
| Weight of empty dish (W1) |  |
| Weight of dish + diosgenin (W2) |  |

% yield of diosgenin = (W2 − W1) × 100 / W

**Worked example.** Powder taken = 20.0 g; diosgenin obtained = 0.42 g.
% yield = 0.42 × 100 / 20 = **2.1% w/w**

## Result

Diosgenin was isolated from *Dioscorea* tubers. Yield = ___% w/w. It gave positive Liebermann–Burchard and Salkowski tests and a TLC spot matching standard diosgenin.

## Precautions

1. Reflux gently and make sure water flows through the condenser before heating.
2. Wash the residue completely free of acid; acid left behind can degrade diosgenin during drying and extraction.
3. Dry the residue fully before Soxhlet extraction; water reduces extraction by petroleum ether.
4. Petroleum ether is highly flammable: heat only on a water bath or mantle, with no naked flame nearby.
5. Add conc. H2SO4 slowly in the colour tests.

## Viva questions

1. **What is dioscin?** The main steroidal saponin of *Dioscorea*; its aglycone is diosgenin.
2. **Why is acid hydrolysis needed?** Diosgenin is bound to sugars; hydrolysis frees the water-insoluble aglycone so it can be taken into a non-polar solvent.
3. **Why is petroleum ether chosen?** It dissolves the non-polar sapogenin and leaves most other plant material behind.
4. **What is the importance of diosgenin?** It is a starting material for steroid hormones; by Marker degradation it gives 16-dehydropregnenolone acetate (16-DPA).
5. **Name two other sources of diosgenin.** Fenugreek seeds and *Costus speciosus*.
6. **Which test shows a steroid nucleus?** Liebermann–Burchard (green-blue) and Salkowski (red chloroform layer).
7. **Why do some manufacturers ferment the tubers first?** The plant's own enzymes partly remove sugars, which improves the yield after acid hydrolysis.

# Isolation and detection of atropine from belladonna

**Aim:** To study the general acid–base scheme by which tropane alkaloids are separated from belladonna leaf, and to detect atropine in the extract by chemical tests and thin layer chromatography.

> Belladonna and its alkaloids are poisons. This exercise is done only in the college laboratory under your teacher's supervision, with the quantities and solvent volumes given in your own lab manual. Wear gloves, never taste any fraction, wash your hands afterwards, and handle organic solvents in a fume cupboard away from flames. The purpose of the exercise is to understand and demonstrate the separation scheme and to identify the alkaloid, not to prepare a quantity of it.

## Principle

Belladonna leaf (*Atropa belladonna* L. or *Atropa acuminata* Royle, family **Solanaceae**) contains a small amount of **tropane alkaloids**, mainly **L-hyoscyamine** with a little **hyoscine**. **Atropine is DL-hyoscyamine**: it is formed when L-hyoscyamine racemises during extraction or on gentle warming with a trace of alkali. That is why the isolated product is usually described as hyoscyamine/atropine.

The separation depends on one simple fact, common to nearly all alkaloids:

| Form | Where it dissolves |
| --- | --- |
| Alkaloid **salt** (in acid) | Water |
| Alkaloid **free base** (in alkali) | Organic solvents such as chloroform or ether |

So moving the alkaloid between an acid aqueous phase and an alkaline organic phase separates it from the fats, chlorophyll, sugars and tannins of the leaf, each time leaving some impurity behind.

```text
Powdered leaf
   │  moisten with an alkali (ammonia or sodium carbonate solution) → free bases
   ↓
Extract with an organic solvent (chloroform or ether)
   │  shake with dilute acid → alkaloid salts pass into the water layer
   ↓
Acid aqueous layer (fats and pigments left in the solvent)
   │  make alkaline with ammonia → free bases again
   ↓
Re-extract with chloroform → evaporate → crude hyoscyamine (with hyoscine)
   │  gentle warming with a trace of alkali
   ↓
Atropine (racemic), identified by its tests
```

## Requirements

**Drug and reagents (quantities as in your lab manual):** powdered belladonna leaf, dilute ammonia solution or sodium carbonate solution, chloroform, dilute sulphuric acid, anhydrous sodium sulphate, fuming nitric acid, acetone, alcoholic potassium hydroxide, Mayer's and Dragendorff's reagents, silica gel G plates and a solvent system from your manual, atropine standard.

**Apparatus:** mortar and pestle, conical flasks, separating funnel, filter papers and funnel, water bath, evaporating dish, TLC chamber and capillaries, UV lamp or spray bottle.

## Procedure (outline)

1. Moisten the powdered leaf with the alkali solution and mix well, so that the alkaloid salts present in the drug are converted to free bases.
2. Extract the moist powder with the organic solvent by the method and for the time stated in your manual, and filter.
3. Shake the filtered solvent extract in a separating funnel with dilute sulphuric acid. The alkaloids move into the acid water layer; pigments and fats stay in the solvent.
4. Separate the acid layer and make it alkaline with ammonia (check with pH paper).
5. Extract the alkaline layer with fresh chloroform. Dry the chloroform layer over anhydrous sodium sulphate.
6. Evaporate the chloroform on a water bath in a fume cupboard. The residue is crude hyoscyamine with hyoscine; warming it gently with a trace of alkali, as directed in your manual, racemises it to atropine.
7. Use a small part of the residue for the identification tests and TLC below. Hand over the rest to your teacher for safe disposal.

## Identification tests

| Test | Procedure | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Vitali–Morin test** | Treat a little residue with fuming nitric acid and evaporate to dryness on a water bath; cool, add acetone and then a drop of alcoholic KOH | **Violet colour** — confirms a tropane ester (atropine, hyoscine) |
| Mayer's reagent | Dissolve a little residue in dilute acid and add the reagent | Cream precipitate (alkaloid) |
| Dragendorff's reagent | As above | Orange-red precipitate (alkaloid) |
| Optical rotation | Polarimeter, if available | Atropine is **racemic and optically inactive**; L-hyoscyamine is laevorotatory |
| TLC | Spot the residue and the atropine standard on silica gel G; develop in the system given in your manual; spray with Dragendorff's reagent | Orange spot with the same Rf as the standard |

## Observations

| Item | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Appearance of the residue | Pale, amorphous to crystalline solid |
| Vitali–Morin test |  |
| Mayer's / Dragendorff's test |  |
| Rf of the sample spot |  |
| Rf of the standard spot |  |

Rf = distance travelled by the spot ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front.

## Result

The alkaloid fraction separated from belladonna leaf gave a positive Vitali–Morin test and a TLC spot with the same Rf as standard atropine, showing that the drug contains tropane alkaloids of the hyoscyamine/atropine type.

## Precautions

1. Treat every fraction as poisonous; do not pipette by mouth and do not taste anything.
2. Keep to the quantities in your lab manual and work only under supervision.
3. Make the aqueous layer properly alkaline before the second extraction, or the alkaloid stays in the water.
4. Vent the separating funnel often and shake gently to avoid emulsions.
5. Fuming nitric acid is corrosive and gives off fumes: use the fume cupboard and add it drop by drop.
6. Evaporate chloroform only on a water bath, never over a flame.
7. Give all residues and solvents to your teacher for proper disposal.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the powder moistened with ammonia first?** To free the alkaloid bases from their salts so they dissolve in the organic solvent.
2. **How is atropine related to hyoscyamine?** Atropine is the racemic (DL) form; the plant contains mainly L-hyoscyamine, which racemises during extraction.
3. **Which test confirms a tropane alkaloid?** The Vitali–Morin test, a violet colour given by tropane esters.
4. **Why is the extract shaken with dilute acid?** The alkaloids pass into the acid water as salts, leaving fats and pigments in the solvent, which purifies the fraction.
5. **How can atropine and hyoscyamine be told apart?** By optical rotation: atropine is optically inactive, hyoscyamine is laevorotatory.
6. **Name two other plants used commercially for tropane alkaloids.** *Duboisia* species and *Hyoscyamus muticus*.
7. **What are the medical uses of atropine sulphate?** As an antimuscarinic: preanaesthetic medication, sinus bradycardia, antidote in organophosphate poisoning, and as a mydriatic and cycloplegic in eye drops.

# Isolation and detection of sennosides from senna

**Aim:** To isolate the sennosides from senna leaf or pods as their calcium salts, find the yield and detect them by Borntrager's test and thin layer chromatography.

> Follow the quantities in your lab manual. Methanol is toxic and flammable; heat it only on a water bath in a fume cupboard.

## Principle

Senna (leaflets or pods of *Cassia angustifolia* Vahl or *C. acutifolia* Delile, family **Leguminosae**) contains **sennosides A, B, C and D**, dianthrone O-glycosides of rhein and aloe-emodin, together with free anthraquinones, flavonoids, mucilage and resins.

- Sennosides are **acidic** glycosides, soluble in aqueous alcohol and in dilute alkali.
- Defatting the drug with a non-polar solvent first removes chlorophyll, fats and resins.
- Extraction with **aqueous methanol** (about 70%) takes out the sennosides; a little acid in the extract keeps them from breaking down.
- The sennosides are then **precipitated as their calcium salts** by adding a calcium salt and adjusting the pH, which separates them from the sugars and other soluble material.
- Identification depends on the anthraquinone nucleus: after hydrolysis and oxidation, the free anthraquinones give the pink-red colour of **Borntrager's test** with ammonia.

```text
Powdered senna ──defat (petroleum ether)──→ marc
   │  extract with 70% aqueous methanol (slightly acidic)
   ↓
Extract ──concentrate under reduced pressure──→ concentrate
   │  add calcium chloride solution, adjust pH with ammonia
   ↓
Calcium sennosides precipitate ──filter, wash with methanol, dry──→ product
```

## Requirements

**Chemicals:** powdered senna leaf or pods, petroleum ether (60–80 °C), methanol, water, dilute hydrochloric acid or citric acid, calcium chloride solution, dilute ammonia solution, ferric chloride solution, benzene or chloroform, silica gel G plates and the solvent system given in your manual, sennoside standard if available.

**Apparatus:** Soxhlet apparatus or percolator, round-bottom flask with reflux condenser, water bath, Buchner funnel with suction, beakers, pH paper, oven or desiccator, TLC chamber.

## Procedure

1. Weigh the powdered drug as directed and defat it with petroleum ether (Soxhlet or by maceration). Discard the petroleum ether extract and air-dry the marc.
2. Extract the marc with about 70% aqueous methanol, kept slightly acidic with a little citric or hydrochloric acid, by refluxing on a water bath. Filter.
3. Repeat the extraction on the residue, and combine the filtrates.
4. Concentrate the combined extract on a water bath (or under reduced pressure) to a small volume.
5. Add calcium chloride solution to the concentrate with stirring, then make it slightly alkaline with dilute ammonia. A brownish precipitate of **calcium sennosides** forms.
6. Allow the precipitate to settle, filter under suction, and wash it with a little methanol to remove colouring matter.
7. Dry the product at a low temperature (in an oven at about 50 °C or in a desiccator), then weigh it.

## Identification tests

| Test | Procedure | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Borntrager's test** | Boil a little product with dilute HCl, cool, shake with benzene or chloroform, separate the organic layer and shake it with dilute ammonia | **Pink to red** ammoniacal layer (anthraquinones) |
| **Modified Borntrager's test** | Boil with ferric chloride in dilute HCl before extracting, then proceed as above | Deeper pink-red colour; the oxidation converts anthranols and dianthrones to anthraquinones |
| Solubility | Shake with dilute sodium bicarbonate solution | Dissolves (acidic glycosides) |
| TLC | Spot the sample and standard on silica gel G; develop in the system from your manual; view in UV 365 nm, or spray with alcoholic potassium hydroxide | Spots with the same Rf as standard sennosides; anthraquinones fluoresce and give a red colour with alkali |

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of senna powder taken (W) |  |
| Weight of filter paper or dish (W1) |  |
| Weight of dish + dry calcium sennosides (W2) |  |

% yield = (W2 − W1) × 100 / W

**Worked example.** Senna powder = 50.0 g; dried calcium sennosides = 0.65 g.
% yield = 0.65 × 100 / 50 = **1.3% w/w**

The product is a mixture of calcium salts of sennosides A, B, C and D with some other material, so its sennoside content is less than 100%. In industry it is assayed spectrophotometrically and expressed as sennoside B.

## Result

Calcium sennosides were isolated from senna. Yield = ___% w/w. The product gave a positive (modified) Borntrager's test and TLC spots matching standard sennosides.

## Precautions

1. Defat the drug first, or the chlorophyll and resin make the final product very dark.
2. Keep the extraction temperature low and the extract slightly acidic; sennosides are degraded by heat and by alkali in the presence of air.
3. Add the ammonia slowly and check the pH; too much alkali dissolves the precipitate again.
4. Wash the precipitate with cold methanol only, since warm methanol dissolves some of the product.
5. Dry at a low temperature.

## Viva questions

1. **What are sennosides?** Dianthrone glycosides of senna; sennosides A and B are stereoisomeric rhein dianthrone glucosides.
2. **Why are they precipitated as calcium salts?** The calcium salts are much less soluble, so they separate cleanly from sugars and other soluble matter, and the salt is stable for formulation.
3. **Why is the plain Borntrager's test weak with senna?** Senna contains mainly dianthrones and anthranols; they must first be oxidised to anthraquinones, which is what the modified test does with ferric chloride.
4. **How do sennosides act as a laxative?** They are not absorbed in the small intestine; colonic bacteria convert them to rhein anthrone, which increases peristalsis and fluid secretion in the colon.
5. **How are sennosides assayed officially?** By a spectrophotometric method in which the aglycones form a red complex with magnesium acetate, read at about 515 nm and calculated as sennoside B; HPLC is used for the individual sennosides.
6. **Which part of the plant is richer in sennosides?** The pods generally contain more than the leaflets.
7. **Name an adulterant of senna leaf.** *Cassia auriculata* leaves (Avaram); dog senna and argel leaves are also reported.

# Separation of sugars by paper chromatography

**Aim:** To separate a mixture of sugars (glucose, fructose, lactose, sucrose) by ascending paper chromatography, to locate the spots with a suitable spray reagent and to calculate the Rf value of each sugar.

> Follow the solvent system and spray reagent given in your lab manual. Aniline and most locating sprays are harmful: use gloves and a fume cupboard, and let your teacher heat the sprayed sheet.

## Principle

Paper chromatography is a **partition** technique. Filter paper is cellulose, which holds a layer of water on its fibres; this bound water is the **stationary phase**. The developing solvent, an organic mixture saturated with water (for example n-butanol : acetic acid : water), is the **mobile phase**.

As the solvent rises by capillary action, each sugar distributes itself between the two liquid phases according to its partition coefficient. A sugar that is more soluble in the mobile phase travels farther; a more water-loving sugar is held back. Sugars are colourless, so the dried sheet is sprayed with a reagent that gives coloured spots: a reducing sugar reacts with **aniline hydrogen phthalate** or with ammoniacal silver nitrate.

**Rf = distance travelled by the solute ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front**

The Rf of a sugar is constant for a given paper, solvent and temperature, so an unknown is identified by running it beside standards.

```text
   solvent front  ── ── ── ── ── ──
                     o  fructose
                  o     glucose
               o        lactose
   baseline  ──x──x──x──x──  (spots applied, above solvent level)
   solvent   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

## Requirements

**Chemicals:** standard solutions (about 1% in water or 10% aqueous isopropanol) of glucose, fructose, lactose and sucrose; a test mixture; n-butanol, glacial acetic acid and water (solvent system, for example 4:1:5, upper layer); spray reagent (aniline hydrogen phthalate in water-saturated butanol, or ammoniacal silver nitrate).

**Apparatus:** Whatman No. 1 chromatography paper, glass chromatographic chamber or wide-mouth jar with a lid, capillary tubes or micropipettes, pencil and scale, stapler or thread, hot air oven, spray bottle, gloves.

## Procedure

1. Cut a strip of Whatman No. 1 paper to fit the chamber. **Handle it by the edges only**; finger marks leave grease spots.
2. Draw a faint **pencil** baseline about 2.5 cm from the lower edge. Mark four or five equally spaced points on it, at least 2 cm apart and 2 cm from the sides.
3. Prepare the mobile phase, shake it in a separating funnel and use the organic (upper) layer. Pour it into the chamber to a depth of about 1 cm and close the lid so the chamber becomes saturated.
4. Apply a small spot of each standard and of the test mixture with a capillary. Keep each spot small (2–3 mm); dry it with cold air and apply again if a stronger spot is needed.
5. Dry the spots completely.
6. Place the paper in the chamber so that the **baseline stays above the solvent level** and the paper does not touch the walls. Close the lid.
7. Allow the solvent to rise until the front is about 2–3 cm from the top (this often takes several hours; some manuals use an overnight run).
8. Remove the paper, mark the **solvent front at once** with a pencil, and dry it in an oven at about 100 °C.
9. Spray evenly with the locating reagent and heat the sheet at about 105 °C for a few minutes until the spots appear.
10. Outline each spot in pencil, mark its centre, and measure the distances.

## Observations and calculation

| Substance | Distance travelled by the spot (cm) | Distance travelled by the solvent front (cm) | Rf |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glucose (standard) |  |  |  |
| Fructose (standard) |  |  |  |
| Lactose (standard) |  |  |  |
| Sucrose (standard) |  |  |  |
| Test mixture — spot 1 |  |  |  |
| Test mixture — spot 2 |  |  |  |

**Worked example.** A spot travels 5.4 cm while the solvent front travels 12.0 cm.
Rf = 5.4 ÷ 12.0 = **0.45**

In a butanol–acetic acid–water system the order of movement is usually the monosaccharides first (fructose a little ahead of glucose), then the disaccharides (sucrose, then lactose), because the larger, more hydroxylated sugars stay in the water phase. Compare the Rf of each unknown spot with that of the standards run on the same sheet, never with a value from a book, since Rf depends on paper, solvent and temperature.

## Result

The sugars in the given mixture were separated by paper chromatography. Their Rf values were ___, ___ and ___, matching standard ______, ______ and ______.

## Precautions

1. Handle the paper by its edges; use a pencil, never ink, for all markings.
2. Keep the spots small and well dried before development, or they will tail and overlap.
3. The baseline must stay above the solvent level, otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent.
4. Saturate the chamber before the run and keep the lid closed throughout.
5. Mark the solvent front immediately after taking the paper out; the solvent evaporates quickly.
6. Spray in a fume cupboard with gloves, and heat only as directed.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the stationary phase in paper chromatography?** The water held on the cellulose fibres of the paper, not the paper itself.
2. **Which mechanism separates the sugars here?** Partition between the bound water and the organic mobile phase.
3. **What is Rf?** The ratio of the distance moved by the solute to the distance moved by the solvent front; it is always less than 1.
4. **Why is the chamber saturated first?** To stop the solvent evaporating from the paper, which would give uneven fronts and poor, irregular Rf values.
5. **Why is acetic acid added to the solvent?** It improves solubility and gives sharper spots by reducing tailing.
6. **Why are sugars not visible without spraying?** They are colourless and do not absorb UV light; the spray forms coloured products with them.
7. **Which sugar does not reduce the silver or aniline reagent readily?** Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so it gives a weaker spot unless it is hydrolysed first.
8. **Name two types of paper chromatography by direction.** Ascending, descending, radial (circular) and two-dimensional.
practicals.title: Separation of sugars by paper chromatography

# Thin layer chromatography of a herbal extract

**Aim:** To prepare a thin layer chromatogram of the given herbal extract on silica gel G, to locate the separated constituents and to calculate their Rf values.

> Use the solvent system and spray reagent given in your lab manual for the drug supplied. Sulphuric acid sprays are corrosive: spray in a fume cupboard with gloves and goggles.

## Principle

Thin layer chromatography (TLC) separates compounds on a thin layer of adsorbent, usually **silica gel G** (G = with calcium sulphate as binder), spread on a glass plate. The silica surface is polar and acts as the **stationary phase**; the developing solvent is the **mobile phase**.

Separation is mainly by **adsorption**. A polar compound is held tightly by the silica and moves little; a less polar compound is held weakly, spends more time in the mobile phase and travels farther. Raising the polarity of the solvent moves everything farther up the plate.

TLC is the standard identity test for herbal drugs: the pattern of spots, their colours and their Rf values make a **fingerprint** that is compared with a standard or with a reference extract.

```text
          solvent front  ── ── ── ── ──
                           o   (least polar, high Rf)
                       o
                   o       (most polar, low Rf)
          baseline ──x────x──   sample | standard
          solvent  ~~~~~~~~~~
```

## Requirements

**Chemicals:** herbal extract (for example an alcoholic extract of senna, turmeric, clove or liquorice), the mobile phase named in your manual (such as toluene : ethyl acetate, or chloroform : methanol), standard marker solution if available, locating reagents — anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid, 10% ethanolic sulphuric acid, Dragendorff's reagent or alcoholic KOH, iodine crystals.

**Apparatus:** silica gel G, glass plates (20 × 5 cm or 20 × 20 cm), TLC spreader or a clean glass rod, oven, TLC chamber with lid, capillary tubes, pencil and scale, UV cabinet (254 and 365 nm), spray bottle.

## Procedure

**A. Preparation of the plate** (or use a ready-made pre-coated plate)

1. Make a slurry of silica gel G with distilled water in the ratio given in your manual (commonly about 1 part gel to 2 parts water) and mix quickly to a smooth paste free of lumps.
2. Spread it on clean, dry plates to a uniform thickness of about 0.25 mm using a spreader.
3. Air-dry the plates, then **activate** them in an oven at about 110 °C for 30 minutes. Cool and store in a desiccator.

**B. Running the chromatogram**

4. Draw a faint pencil baseline about 1.5–2 cm from the lower edge and mark the points of application.
5. Apply small spots of the extract (and the standard beside it) with a capillary, keeping each spot 2–3 mm wide. Dry between applications.
6. Pour the mobile phase into the chamber to a depth of about 1 cm, line it with filter paper and close the lid to saturate it.
7. Place the plate so the baseline is **above** the solvent level, close the lid and let the solvent rise until the front is about 1–2 cm from the top.
8. Remove the plate, mark the solvent front at once and dry it.

**C. Detection**

9. Examine first under **UV 254 nm** (dark spots on a fluorescent plate) and **UV 365 nm** (fluorescent spots). Outline the spots in pencil.
10. Then use a chemical method: iodine vapour in a closed jar (brown spots, non-destructive), or spray with the reagent for the class of compounds concerned and heat as directed.

| Class of constituent | Usual spray | Colour of spots |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Terpenoids, volatile oils | Anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid, heat 105 °C | Blue, violet, pink, grey |
| Alkaloids | Dragendorff's reagent | Orange to reddish-brown |
| Anthraquinone glycosides | Alcoholic KOH (or ammonia vapour) | Pink to red |
| Flavonoids | Aluminium chloride, view in UV 365 nm | Yellow fluorescence |
| Steroids, triterpenoids | Liebermann–Burchard reagent, heat | Green, blue or pink |
| General (non-specific) | Iodine vapour, or 10% ethanolic H2SO4 with heating | Brown; charred dark spots |

## Observations and calculation

| Spot | Colour / appearance | Distance moved by spot (cm) | Distance moved by solvent front (cm) | Rf |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |  |
| Standard |  |  |  |  |

Rf = distance travelled by the spot ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front

**Worked example.** Spot moves 6.0 cm, solvent front 8.0 cm → Rf = 6.0 ÷ 8.0 = **0.75**

Some books also report the **Rx** value, the Rf of the spot divided by the Rf of a reference substance run on the same plate.

## Result

The given herbal extract gave ___ spots on silica gel G with the mobile phase used. Their Rf values were ___, ___ and ___; the spot at Rf ___ corresponds to the standard ______.

## Precautions

1. Clean the plates well; grease spoils the layer and the run.
2. Spread an even layer and activate the plates before use, since adsorbed moisture lowers the activity of silica.
3. Keep spots small, and far enough apart that they do not merge.
4. The baseline must remain above the solvent level.
5. Saturate the chamber and keep the lid closed during development.
6. Mark the solvent front immediately after removing the plate.
7. Spray only in a fume cupboard; heat charring sprays uniformly on a hot plate.

## Viva questions

1. **What does the "G" in silica gel G mean?** It contains calcium sulphate (gypsum) as a binder.
2. **Which mechanism works in TLC on silica?** Mainly adsorption, though partition also plays a part on some layers.
3. **Why are the plates activated at 110 °C?** To drive off adsorbed moisture, which would otherwise deactivate the silica and lower reproducibility.
4. **What is a TLC fingerprint?** The whole pattern of spots, colours and Rf values of an extract, used to identify a herbal drug and to check batch-to-batch consistency.
5. **Give two advantages of TLC over paper chromatography.** Faster runs with sharper spots, and corrosive sprays and heating can be used because the layer is inorganic.
6. **What is HPTLC?** High performance TLC — fine, uniform pre-coated plates with automatic application and a densitometric scanner, which allows quantitative work.
7. **How can spots be seen without any reagent?** Under UV light, or with iodine vapour, which is non-destructive so the compound can be recovered.
8. **Why must the chamber be saturated?** To prevent solvent evaporating from the plate surface, which distorts the front and changes Rf values.

# Distillation of volatile oils and detection of constituents by TLC

**Aim:** To obtain the volatile oil of a given drug (clove, fennel, coriander, cinnamon or mint) by hydrodistillation using a Clevenger apparatus, to find the percentage yield, and to detect its chief constituents by thin layer chromatography.

> Use the quantity of drug and the distillation time given in your lab manual. Check that the condenser water is running before heating, and never heat a closed apparatus.

## Principle

A **volatile (essential) oil** is a mixture of terpenoids and phenylpropanoids that evaporates at room temperature and is immiscible with water.

When a mixture of two immiscible liquids is heated, each exerts its own vapour pressure, and the mixture boils when the **sum** of the two vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure. This happens below the boiling point of either liquid, so the oil distils over with the steam well below 100 °C even though many of its constituents boil above 200 °C. This is how heat-sensitive oils are distilled without decomposing.

The vapours condense, and in the **Clevenger** graduated side-arm the oil separates from the water by density, so the volume can be read directly. The apparatus has two patterns, one for oils lighter than water (clove leaf, mint, fennel, coriander) and one for oils heavier than water (clove bud oil and cinnamon bark oil are heavier).

TLC then separates the constituents of the oil, which are identified by their Rf values and by the colours given with **anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid** spray.

```text
Drug + water in flask ──heat──→ steam + oil vapour ──condenser──→ 
        graduated tube: oil layer over (or under) water → read volume
```

## Requirements

**Drug:** coarsely powdered or crushed clove, fennel, coriander, cinnamon bark or fresh mint leaves.

**Chemicals:** distilled water, anhydrous sodium sulphate, toluene and ethyl acetate (mobile phase, for example 93:7), anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid spray reagent, ferric chloride solution, standard eugenol/anethole if available.

**Apparatus:** Clevenger apparatus with a round-bottom flask (1 litre), heating mantle, anti-bumping granules, measuring cylinder, small sample vials, silica gel G plates, TLC chamber, capillaries, hot air oven, spray bottle.

## Procedure

**A. Distillation**

1. Weigh the drug (for example 25–50 g of crushed clove) and transfer it to the round-bottom flask.
2. Add enough distilled water to cover the drug well, plus a few anti-bumping granules.
3. Fit the Clevenger apparatus (choose the pattern suited to an oil lighter or heavier than water) and fill the graduated side arm with water as directed.
4. Start the condenser water, then heat the flask with a mantle. Keep the boiling gentle and steady.
5. Distil for the time given in your manual (commonly 3–4 hours), until no further increase in the volume of oil is seen in the graduated tube over about 30 minutes.
6. Stop heating, let the apparatus cool, read the **volume of oil** in the graduated tube, and run it into a vial.
7. Dry the oil with a pinch of anhydrous sodium sulphate, decant into a clean vial, label it and keep it closed in the dark.

**B. Examination of the oil**

8. Note its colour, odour and whether it is lighter or heavier than water.
9. Place a drop on filter paper; a volatile oil evaporates and leaves **no permanent translucent stain**, unlike a fixed oil.
10. Clove or cinnamon oil with ferric chloride gives a blue colour (phenolic eugenol).

**C. TLC**

11. Dissolve one drop of the oil in about 1 ml toluene.
12. Spot it on an activated silica gel G plate beside the standard, if available.
13. Develop in toluene : ethyl acetate (93:7) or the system given in your manual, in a saturated chamber.
14. Dry the plate, spray with anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid and heat at about 105 °C for 5 minutes.
15. Mark the coloured spots and calculate their Rf values.

| Oil | Main constituent to look for | Usual colour after spray |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clove | Eugenol | Brown to violet |
| Cinnamon bark | Cinnamaldehyde | Blue-violet to grey |
| Fennel | Anethole (also fenchone) | Violet to grey |
| Coriander | Linalool | Blue to violet |
| Mint | Menthol (also menthone) | Blue to violet |

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of drug taken (W g) |  |
| Volume of oil collected (V ml) |  |
| Colour and odour of the oil |  |
| Behaviour on filter paper |  |

% yield of volatile oil (v/w) = V × 100 / W

**Worked example.** Clove taken = 40.0 g; oil collected = 6.2 ml.
% yield = 6.2 × 100 / 40 = **15.5% v/w**

Rf of each spot = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front.

## Result

The volatile oil of the given drug was obtained by hydrodistillation. Yield = ___% v/w. The oil gave ___ spots on TLC; the spot at Rf ___ corresponds to ______, the main constituent of the oil.

## Precautions

1. Start the condenser water before heating, and keep it flowing throughout.
2. Never heat a closed system; the apparatus must stay open to air at the top of the condenser.
3. Use anti-bumping granules and gentle, steady heating; violent boiling throws drug into the condenser.
4. Choose the correct Clevenger pattern for an oil lighter or heavier than water.
5. Read the volume only after the apparatus has cooled and the layers have separated cleanly.
6. Dry the oil over anhydrous sodium sulphate and store it in a well-filled, closed amber vial, since volatile oils oxidise and resinify in air and light.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does a volatile oil distil below 100 °C with water?** The two liquids are immiscible, so the mixture boils when the sum of their vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure, which happens below the boiling point of either.
2. **Why is this better than simple distillation for essential oils?** The constituents would decompose at their own boiling points, which are much higher.
3. **How do you tell a volatile oil from a fixed oil?** A volatile oil evaporates completely from filter paper and leaves no permanent stain; it also has a characteristic odour and does not saponify in the ordinary way.
4. **What does the Clevenger apparatus do?** It condenses the distillate and collects the oil in a graduated side arm so its volume is read directly, with the water returning to the flask.
5. **Which clove oil is heavier than water?** Clove bud oil, because it is rich in eugenol; cinnamon bark oil is also heavier.
6. **Which spray reagent is general for volatile oils on TLC?** Anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid, followed by heating.
7. **Name three other extraction methods for volatile oils.** Expression (citrus peel), enfleurage or solvent extraction (delicate flowers) and supercritical carbon dioxide extraction.
8. **Why is the oil stored in a filled amber bottle?** To keep out light and air, which cause oxidation and resinification.

# Analysis of crude drugs by chemical tests: asafoetida, benzoin, colophony, aloes and myrrh

**Aim:** To identify asafoetida, benzoin, colophony, aloes and myrrh by their characteristic chemical tests.

> Follow your lab manual where details differ. Conc. sulphuric acid, nitric acid and bromine are corrosive and give off fumes: work in a fume cupboard, wear gloves and goggles, and add acids drop by drop.

## Principle

These five are **unorganised drugs** — resins, oleo-gum-resins, a balsamic resin and a dried juice. They have no cells to examine, so identification rests on their behaviour with solvents and on colour reactions of their main constituents:

| Drug | Type | Key constituent tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asafoetida | Oleo-gum-resin | Umbelliferone (combined), ferulic acid esters, sulphur compounds |
| Benzoin | Balsamic resin | Benzoic acid (Siam) and cinnamic acid (Sumatra) and their esters |
| Colophony | Resin proper | Abietic acid and related resin acids |
| Aloes | Dried juice | Aloin, a C-glycoside of aloe-emodin anthrone |
| Myrrh | Oleo-gum-resin | Furanosesquiterpenes of the volatile oil |

A gum + resin mixture (asafoetida, myrrh) forms an **emulsion** when triturated with water, because the gum emulsifies the resin and oil. A resin proper (colophony) does not. Benzoin, being a balsam of benzoic/cinnamic acid esters, gives a **sublimate of benzoic acid** on heating. Aloin is a C-glycoside, so the ordinary Borntrager's test fails and the **modified** test must be used.

## Requirements

**Drugs:** asafoetida, benzoin (Sumatra and Siam if available), colophony, aloes (Curacao and Cape if available), myrrh.

**Reagents:** conc. sulphuric acid, conc. and 50% nitric acid, conc. hydrochloric acid, dilute hydrochloric acid, ammonia solution, potassium permanganate solution, borax solution, bromine water, ferric chloride solution, copper acetate solution (dilute), light petroleum, ether, benzene or chloroform, 90% alcohol, acetic anhydride.

**Apparatus:** test tubes and holders, mortar and pestle, watch glasses, dry test tube for sublimation, water bath, spirit lamp, filter papers and funnel, separating funnel or stoppered test tubes, UV lamp.

## Procedure and observations

### 1. Asafoetida

| Test | Procedure | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emulsion test | Triturate a little drug with water in a mortar | Milky white emulsion | Gum + resin + oil (oleo-gum-resin) |
| Sulphuric acid | Touch a fresh fracture with conc. H2SO4 | Red to reddish-brown colour | Resin (asaresinotannol) |
| Nitric acid | Add 50% HNO3 to a little drug | Green colour | Asafoetida |
| **Umbelliferone test** | Boil about 0.5 g with dilute HCl, cool, filter and make the filtrate alkaline with ammonia; view in daylight or UV | **Blue fluorescence** | Umbelliferone set free from its combined form |
| Odour | Smell cautiously | Strong persistent garlic-like odour | Organic sulphur compounds |

A sample showing umbelliferone fluorescence **before** hydrolysis suggests adulteration with galbanum, in which umbelliferone is free.

### 2. Benzoin

| Test | Procedure | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sublimation | Heat a little powder gently in a dry test tube | White crystalline sublimate on the cooler walls | Benzoic acid (and cinnamic acid) |
| **Permanganate test** | Warm about 0.5 g with 5 ml KMnO4 solution | Odour of **benzaldehyde** (bitter almond) | Cinnamic acid → **Sumatra** benzoin. No such odour → Siam benzoin |
| Solubility | Shake with 90% alcohol; then add water to the solution | Dissolves in alcohol; milky emulsion on adding water | Resin, insoluble in water |
| Ferric chloride | Alcoholic solution + FeCl3 | Green colour with Siam benzoin (coniferyl benzoate) | Variety test |

### 3. Colophony

| Test | Procedure | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emulsion test | Triturate with water | **No emulsion** | Resin proper, no gum |
| Solubility | Shake with alcohol, then with water | Soluble in alcohol, insoluble in water | Resin |
| **Copper acetate test** | Dissolve a little in light petroleum, shake with dilute copper acetate solution, allow to separate | **Emerald-green** colour in the petroleum layer | Copper abietate (abietic acid) |
| Liebermann–Burchard type test | Dissolve in acetic anhydride and add a drop of conc. H2SO4 | Purple-violet colour that fades quickly | Resin acids |
| Flame | Heat a small piece on a spatula | Burns with a smoky flame | Resin |

### 4. Aloes

| Test | Procedure | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Modified Borntrager's test** | Boil about 0.5 g with dilute HCl and a little ferric chloride solution for a few minutes; cool, shake with benzene or chloroform; separate the organic layer and shake it with dilute ammonia | **Pink to red** ammoniacal layer | Anthraquinones released from the **C-glycoside** aloin (plain Borntrager's test fails) |
| **Borax (Schouteten's) test** | Warm a little aqueous solution with borax solution; view under UV | Green fluorescence | Aloe-emodin anthranol |
| Bromine test | Add bromine water to an aqueous solution | Pale yellow precipitate | Tetrabromaloin |
| Nitric acid test | Add conc. HNO3 to the powder on a watch glass | Deep reddish-brown with **Curacao**; brownish then fading with **Cape** | Distinguishes varieties |
| Cupraloin test | Aqueous solution + copper sulphate solution, sodium chloride and 90% alcohol; warm | Wine-red colour with Curacao aloes | Isobarbaloin present |

### 5. Myrrh

| Test | Procedure | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emulsion test | Triturate with water | Yellowish-brown emulsion | Oleo-gum-resin |
| **Bromine (or nitric acid) test** | Extract a little drug with ether, evaporate a few drops of the extract on a watch glass and expose the residue to bromine vapour, or add conc. HNO3 | **Violet** colour | Furanosesquiterpenes |
| Sulphuric acid | Touch the powder with conc. H2SO4 | Reddish-violet colour | Resin |
| Odour and taste | Smell; taste cautiously only if permitted | Aromatic odour, bitter acrid taste | Myrrh |

## Result

The given samples were identified as **asafoetida, benzoin, colophony, aloes and myrrh** on the basis of the tests above, the confirmatory ones being the umbelliferone fluorescence (asafoetida), the benzaldehyde odour with permanganate and the benzoic acid sublimate (benzoin), the emerald-green copper acetate test (colophony), the modified Borntrager's test (aloes) and the violet colour with bromine vapour (myrrh).

## Precautions

1. Work in a fume cupboard; conc. acids and bromine give harmful fumes.
2. Add acids drop by drop down the side of a slanted tube, and never add water to conc. acid.
3. Heat test tubes on a water bath wherever possible, mouth pointed away from everyone.
4. Use small quantities of drug; these drugs give strong colours even in traces.
5. Use a fresh fracture of asafoetida for the acid colour tests, since the surface is oxidised.
6. For the modified Borntrager's test, the ferric chloride must be present during boiling; otherwise the C-glycoside is not split and the test fails.
7. Smell by wafting the vapour towards you, never by putting the tube to your nose.

## Viva questions

1. **What is an oleo-gum-resin?** A natural exudate containing resin, volatile oil and gum, for example asafoetida, myrrh and guggul.
2. **Why does asafoetida form an emulsion with water?** Its gum fraction emulsifies the resin and volatile oil.
3. **Why does aloes need the modified Borntrager's test?** Aloin is a C-glycoside; the C–C bond is not broken by acid alone, so ferric chloride is added to oxidise and split it to free anthraquinones.
4. **How do you distinguish Sumatra from Siam benzoin?** Sumatra benzoin contains cinnamic acid and gives the benzaldehyde odour on warming with potassium permanganate; Siam benzoin does not.
5. **What is the copper acetate test for?** Colophony: abietic acid forms green copper abietate, which dissolves in the petroleum layer.
6. **Why does colophony give no emulsion with water?** It is a resin proper, with no gum to act as an emulsifier.
7. **Name the chief chemical constituents of myrrh's volatile oil.** Furanosesquiterpenes such as furanoeudesma-1,3-diene and curzerene.
8. **Which test shows adulteration of asafoetida with galbanum?** Free umbelliferone fluorescence without prior hydrolysis.
9. **Name two adulterants of asafoetida.** Colophony, gum arabic, sand, red clay and stones have all been reported.

1. Primary metabolites are needed for the life of every cell; secondary metabolites are not essential for the cell's own survival.
2. Primary metabolites occur in all plants; secondary metabolites occur only in certain species, organs or stages.
3. Primary: carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids. Secondary: alkaloids, glycosides, terpenoids, flavonoids, tannins, resins.
4. Primary metabolites are produced in large amounts and vary little; secondary metabolites are produced in small amounts and vary with season, climate and plant part.
5. Secondary metabolites protect the plant and attract pollinators, and most medicinal activity belongs to them, for example morphine, digoxin, menthol and quercetin.

1. Acetyl-CoA is carboxylated to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
2. A starter unit is joined head-to-tail with several malonyl-CoA units; carbon dioxide is lost at each step, so the chain grows by two carbons each time.
3. If each keto group is reduced as the chain grows, a fatty acid is formed, for example palmitic and oleic acids.
4. If the keto groups are not reduced, a poly-beta-keto chain (polyketide) is formed, which folds and cyclises by aldol or Claisen reactions into aromatic rings.
5. Products: anthraquinones of senna, aloes, rhubarb and cascara; phloroglucinols and chromones; ring A of flavonoids; microbial polyketides such as tetracyclines and griseofulvin.

questions.answer:
1. Synonym: afim, raw opium.
2. Biological source: dried latex obtained by incising the unripe capsules of Papaver somniferum L., family Papaveraceae.
3. Geographical source: India is a major licit producer, with licensed cultivation in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh; also Turkey and Australia (as poppy straw).
4. Collection: a few days after the petals fall, when the capsules turn yellowish-green, shallow vertical incisions are made in the afternoon with a multi-bladed knife; the latex that exudes coagulates overnight and is scraped off next morning, then dried and made into cakes.
5. Chemical constituents: about 25 alkaloids, mostly combined with meconic acid.
   - phenanthrene group: morphine (the main alkaloid, about 10%), codeine, thebaine;
   - benzylisoquinoline group: papaverine, noscapine (narcotine), narceine;
   - also meconic acid, sugars, resin, wax and mucilage.
6. Chemical test: an aqueous extract with ferric chloride gives a deep red colour due to meconic acid, which is not discharged by dilute hydrochloric acid.
7. Uses: morphine for severe pain; codeine as an antitussive and mild analgesic; papaverine as a smooth muscle relaxant; noscapine as an antitussive; thebaine as a raw material for semi-synthetic opioids and antagonists. Opium preparations were formerly used in diarrhoea.
8. Commercial applications: opium and poppy straw are the raw materials of alkaloid factories; poppy seeds and poppy seed oil are used in food, and contain almost no alkaloid.
9. Legal control: opium, poppy straw and their alkaloids are controlled under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985; cultivation requires a licence from the Central Bureau of Narcotics.
